anchor: As I lay asleep in Italy
title: Occasion: Peterloo
short: Written in September 1819 in Italy after news of the Peterloo Massacre (Manchester, 16 August 1819); sent to Leigh Hunt but not published until 1832.
body: On 16 August 1819 a peaceful crowd of perhaps 60,000 gathered in St Peter's Field, Manchester, to hear the radical Henry Hunt speak for parliamentary reform; local yeomanry and then regular hussars charged with sabres, killing some fifteen to eighteen people and injuring hundreds. The press named it 'Peterloo' in mockery of Waterloo. Shelley, living near Livorno, heard in early September and wrote to Ollier that his indignation was still boiling. He sent the poem to Leigh Hunt for The Examiner, but Hunt, fearing prosecution for seditious libel, held it back until 1832, the year of the Reform Act. The dream-vision opening ('a voice from over the Sea') frames the poem as a visionary report from exile.

title: Mask / masque
short: The title puns on 'mask', a disguise, and 'masque', a courtly pageant; the following procession is a masquerade of state violence.
body: Shelley's manuscript title is 'The Mask of Anarchy', and Hunt printed it in 1832 as 'The Masque of Anarchy'. Both senses operate. A masque was an aristocratic entertainment of allegorical figures in procession, and Shelley turns it into a 'ghastly masquerade' (l. 27) in which Murder, Fraud and Hypocrisy wear the faces of ministers. The masks also reverse the expected direction of disguise: the vices are not hidden behind respectable faces, but the respectable faces are revealed as masks of vice. The device owes something to the popular satirical prints of the period, in which politicians appeared as allegorical monsters.

anchor: I met Murder on the way
title: Murder ... Castlereagh
short: Robert Stewart, Viscount Castlereagh, Foreign Secretary and leader of the Commons, associated with the brutal suppression of the Irish rising of 1798.
body: Castlereagh (1769-1822) was the government's chief spokesman in the House of Commons and had been Chief Secretary for Ireland when the 1798 rebellion was put down with great severity; radicals regarded him as the embodiment of reaction at home and abroad, through the Congress of Vienna and the Holy Alliance. Shelley makes him Murder, 'Very smooth' yet grim, feeding human hearts to seven fat bloodhounds; editors have tried to identify the hounds with the allied powers of the post-Napoleonic settlement, though the reference is not certain. Byron attacked Castlereagh with similar violence in the dedication to Don Juan written the year before.

title: Fraud ... Eldon
short: John Scott, Lord Eldon, Lord Chancellor, notorious for weeping in court; in 1817 his Chancery judgment took Shelley's two children by Harriet from him.
body: The ermined gown is the robe of the Lord Chancellor. Eldon (1751-1838) was known for tears on the bench and for interminable delays in Chancery. After Harriet Shelley's suicide in 1816, her family petitioned to keep her children from Shelley, citing his atheism and his views on marriage, and in March 1817 Eldon ruled against him; Shelley had already cursed him in the poem 'To the Lord Chancellor'. Here the Chancellor's tears turn to millstones that dash out children's brains, a grotesque image that mixes private grievance with public charge, since the legal system was seen as crushing the poor.

title: Hypocrisy ... Sidmouth ... crocodile
short: Henry Addington, Lord Sidmouth, Home Secretary, who ran a network of spies and supported a grant for building new churches; he rides a crocodile, emblem of false tears.
body: As Home Secretary (1812-22) Sidmouth was responsible for internal security: the suspension of habeas corpus in 1817, the use of informers and agents provocateurs, and the congratulations sent to the Manchester magistrates after Peterloo. 'Clothed with the Bible' glances at his support for the Church Building Act of 1818, which granted a million pounds for new Anglican churches in the growing towns, while the poor went hungry. The crocodile, which proverbially weeps as it devours, completes the image of piety masking cruelty. The following stanza extends the parade to 'Bishops, lawyers, peers, or spies'.

title: spies
short: The list ends with spies: the government's informers, notably 'Oliver the Spy', whose provocation preceded the Pentrich rising of 1817.
body: In 1817 a government agent, W. J. Richards, known as Oliver, encouraged plans for an armed rising in Derbyshire; its leaders were hanged and beheaded in November 1817, and the exposure of Oliver's role in the radical press caused a scandal. Shelley responded with his pamphlet An Address to the People on the Death of the Princess Charlotte, which contrasted national mourning for the princess with the executions. The line's flat list sets the established professions (church, law, aristocracy) beside paid informers, as equally disguised instruments of 'Destructions'.

anchor: On a white horse, splashed with blood
title: Anarchy ... Like Death in the Apocalypse
short: Anarchy rides like Death on the pale horse of Revelation 6:8; Shelley's twist is to call lawless government, not popular revolt, 'Anarchy'.
body: In Revelation 6:8 the fourth horseman, on a pale horse, is named Death, and Hell follows him. Shelley's Anarchy is the climax of the procession, crowned and sceptred, and the irony is pointed: conservatives used 'anarchy' for the threat of revolution, but here the ruling order itself is lawless violence, trampling 'The adoring multitude'. The inscription on his brow, 'I AM GOD, AND KING, AND LAW', recalls the names written on the harlot's forehead and on the rider's vesture in Revelation (compare 17:5 and 19:16) and parodies the alliance of throne, altar and courts. The anarchist philosopher William Godwin, Shelley's father-in-law, had argued that government itself is the chief source of disorder.

anchor: I AM GOD, AND KING, AND LAW
title: I AM GOD, AND KING, AND LAW
short: The motto unites the three powers Shelley attacked throughout his work: established religion, monarchy and the law used as an instrument of the rich.
body: The phrase is repeated and reshuffled by the hired soldiers ('Thou art God, and Law, and King'), by lawyers and priests ('Thou art Law and God'), and by all ('Thou art King, and God, and Lord'), until the litany ends in a parody of the Lord's Prayer, 'Be thy name made holy now'. The rearrangements suggest that the terms are interchangeable masks of one power. Scrivener reads the poem as an expression of Shelley's philosophical anarchism, derived from Godwin, in which these institutions are forms of a single domination. The later stanzas define a true 'Law' against this one, in the 'old laws of England'.

anchor: To seize upon the Bank and Tower
title: the Bank and Tower ... pensioned Parliament
short: Anarchy plans a coup: the Bank of England, the Tower of London and a Parliament of pensioners; the irony recalls the Spa Fields plot of 1816.
body: In December 1816 a breakaway group from a radical meeting at Spa Fields, London, marched towards the City with talk of seizing the Tower and the Bank; the government made much of the episode to justify repression. Shelley reverses the charge: the real conspirators against the nation's wealth and arms are its rulers. The 'pensioned Parliament' refers to the placemen and holders of government pensions and sinecures who, radicals complained, filled the unreformed House of Commons. The procession is about to take its seat when Hope interrupts it.

title: a maniac maid ... Hope
short: Hope, mad with grief and looking like Despair, is the last surviving child of Time; she lies down before the horses in passive defiance.
body: Her father Time is old, 'idiot-like' and palsied, worn out with waiting for a better day; all his children but her are dead. The image reverses the classical Time who devours his children (Kronos/Saturn) into a feeble parent who has outlived them. Hope's act, lying down in the street before the cavalry, is an early figure for the non-violent resistance the poem later recommends to the crowd. Some critics have seen in it a memory of the women at Peterloo, several of whom were among the killed and wounded. Her transformation into 'Hope, that maiden most serene' (l. 128) marks the turn of the poem.

title: a Shape arrayed in mail
short: A mist grows into an armoured, winged Shape crowned with the morning star; it passes invisibly, and thoughts spring up wherever it treads.
body: The Shape is never named. Critics variously identify it as the spirit of Liberty, of the people's collective will, or of revolutionary thought; its effect is psychological rather than physical, since men feel its presence but see 'empty air', and the consequence is the birth of 'Thoughts'. The helmet's planet 'like the Morning's' is Venus as morning star, Lucifer, 'light-bearer', a sign of a new day, and it rains 'crimson dew' through its plumes. The stanza of similes that follows ('As flowers beneath May's footstep waken') belongs to Shelley's recurring imagery of regeneration, close to that of Prometheus Unbound, written in the same year.

title: A planet, like the Morning's
short: The morning star, Venus, is the herald of dawn; Shelley uses it often as an emblem of hope and liberty (compare Lucifer in Isaiah 14:12).
body: In the KJV, Isaiah 14:12 addresses the fallen king of Babylon as 'O Lucifer, son of the morning', a text later applied to Satan; Shelley, like Blake, tended to reverse the orthodox valuation and treat the light-bringer as a figure of rebellion against tyranny. In The Revolt of Islam (1817) the morning star appears as a positive symbol in the opening canto. Here the planet on the Shape's helmet promises the dawn that follows the night of the procession, and its light, filtered through plumes, falls as 'crimson dew', an image that anticipates the refrain's chains shaken off 'like dew'.

title: Rise like Lions after slumber
short: The refrain calls on the English to rise in their numbers, echoing Milton's image of a nation rousing itself like a strong man after sleep.
body: Milton's Areopagitica (1644) pictures England as a noble nation 'rousing herself like a strong man after sleep, and shaking her invincible locks', the figure of Samson. Shelley's lions waking and shaking off chains 'like dew' combine strength with ease: the chains are as insubstantial as the dew that fell in the night of sleep, so oppression depends on the people's passivity. The refrain frames the long speech of the Earth (ll. 147-372) and gives the poem its most famous line, 'Ye are many, they are few', which has been taken up by later radical and labour movements.

title: Ye are many, they are few
short: The arithmetic of revolution: the oppressed vastly outnumber their oppressors, whose power rests on the many's consent.
body: The idea had a long radical pedigree; it is close to David Hume's observation, in 'Of the First Principles of Government' (1741), that the many are governed by the few only through opinion, and to the writings of Paine and Godwin. Shelley gives it the force of a slogan by its brevity and its place as the extra fifth line of the refrain stanza. It has often been quoted at political rallies, and Jeremy Corbyn quoted the closing stanza at Glastonbury in 2017, and some commentators have suggested that the title of Labour's 2017 manifesto, 'For the Many, Not the Few', echoes it, though that wording had stood in the party's Clause IV since 1995. Its meaning in context, though, is followed by a call to non-violent assembly rather than armed rising.

title: Paper coin, that forgery
short: An attack on paper money: since 1797 the Bank of England had not exchanged its notes for gold, and radicals such as Cobbett called paper currency a fraud on labour.
body: The Bank Restriction Act of 1797 suspended the convertibility of banknotes into gold to finance the war against France; it was ended only by Peel's Act of 1819, passed shortly before Peterloo. Cobbett's Paper against Gold (1810-11) argued that paper money and the national debt transferred wealth from labourers to fundholders. Shelley develops the same case in A Philosophical View of Reform (1819-20). Here the 'Ghost of Gold', paper credit, takes from toil a thousandfold more than gold ever did, and paper money is called a forgery of the title-deeds to the people's 'inheritance of Earth'.

anchor: to quench thy flame in Gaul
title: Leagued to quench thy flame in Gaul
short: The wars of the European monarchies against Revolutionary France (1793-1815) are presented as wars against Liberty, which they dimmed but could not extinguish.
body: 'Gaul' is the Latin name for France. In Shelley's radical reading, the coalitions formed against France from 1792 were a league of kings to crush the Revolution's liberty; English 'toil and blood' were poured out for that end, and the national debt contracted to pay for it weighed on the poor. Shelley elsewhere, notably in the preface to The Revolt of Islam, analysed how the Revolution's excesses had produced despair among its former sympathisers, and he insists here that liberty was dimmed but not put out.

title: Let a great Assembly be
short: The Earth calls for a vast peaceful meeting on open ground, a deliberate re-enactment of St Peter's Field, under the witness of sky and earth.
body: The remedy proposed is not insurrection but a lawful mass meeting, of the kind the Manchester crowd had attended, gathered from every corner of the country, from workhouses, prisons and even palaces. The assembly is to declare 'with measured words' that its members are free; its words should wound like swords and protect like 'targes'. The poem thus defends the right of public assembly, which the government's Six Acts of December 1819 would restrict. Scholars disagree whether this programme is a realistic political strategy, a visionary ideal, or a deliberately restrained proposal fitted to a newspaper audience.

title: targes
short: 'Targes' are light round shields; the people's words are to be both weapons and protection.
body: 'Targe' is an old word for a shield, especially the small round shield of the Highland soldier, and the diminutive 'target' first meant the same. The image balances the previous line, in which words are 'Keen to wound as sharpened swords', so that speech serves both as attack and as defence. It fits the poem's trust in persuasion: the assembled people resist by declaration and by their moral authority, not by arms.

anchor: With folded arms and steady eyes
title: With folded arms and steady eyes
short: The people are to meet the soldiers' charge without resistance, so that the tyrants' shame does the work; critics debate whether this is pacifism or strategy.
body: The Earth's speech tells the crowd to stand 'calm and resolute, / Like a forest close and mute', to let the soldiers 'Slash, and stab, and maim, and hew', and to watch until their rage dies away; the shed blood will then speak 'In hot blushes on their cheek', women will scorn them, and soldiers will desert to the people. Some readers see a principled doctrine of passive resistance, later admired by campaigners for non-violent protest. Others, such as Paul Foot, read the advice tactically, as a way of seizing moral advantage, and note the threat of retribution ('A volcano heard afar'). The stanza's plain diction turns Peterloo itself into a model rather than a defeat.

title: The old laws of England
short: Shelley appeals to an idealised ancient constitution, the rule of law and the liberties of 'a wiser day', against the present government.
body: Radicals of the period often appealed to the 'ancient constitution' and to Magna Carta and the Bill of Rights as guarantees of freedom from arbitrary power, claiming that reform restored rather than overthrew English liberty. Shelley's Earth personifies these laws as gray-headed elders whose voice must echo 'Liberty', and lays the blame for any bloodshed on whoever first violates them. The appeal to law is tactical as well as sincere: it puts the people on the side of legality and the magistrates outside it. It contrasts with Anarchy's motto 'LAW' at the start of the poem.

title: Eloquent, oracular; / A volcano heard afar
short: The slaughter will rise like inspiration, like the steam of an oracle, and rumble like a distant volcano: a warning of eruption if wrongs continue.
body: The image mixes the Delphic oracle, whose priestess was said to prophesy from vapours rising out of the earth, with the volcano, a favourite Romantic figure for revolution. Shelley had visited Vesuvius in December 1818 and wrote about it in his letters. The volcano is 'heard afar', so the effect is a menacing promise rather than an explosion within the poem. The stanza thus qualifies the non-violent advice that precedes it, a balance critics read differently.

anchor: There came a voice from over the Sea
title: Metre and stanza
short: Mostly four-stress couplets in quatrains, with occasional five-line stanzas; the popular, ballad-like form was chosen to reach a wide audience.
body: The poem's 372 lines use a short, emphatic line of seven or eight syllables, often trochaic in rhythm, rhymed in couplets (aabb), with some stanzas extended to five lines by a third rhyme. The measure resembles popular broadside verse and hymns, and Shelley wrote to Hunt in late 1819 of his wish to produce a volume of popular songs for the people; poems such as 'Song to the Men of England' belong to the same project. Hunt's 1832 preface praised the poem's directness. The plain style contrasts with the dense symbolism of Prometheus Unbound, composed in the same year.
